featured.title: Four Commodity Vessels Cross Hormuz as Shipping Crisis Deepens
featured.content: The Strait of Hormuz is experiencing one of its sharpest reductions in commercial traffic since the Middle East conflict began. Kpler data cited by Reuters shows only four commodity vessels passed through the waterway on Monday, compared with around 125 daily transits before the conflict. The disruption is increasing pressure on global oil markets, with Brent and US crude both rising again.

articles.title: Hormuz Shipping Falls to Four Commodity Vessels
articles.content: Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz has fallen to critically low levels. Reuters reports that only four commodity vessels crossed the waterway on Monday, compared with ten the previous day and roughly 125 daily transits before the conflict. The strait normally carries a major share of global crude oil and liquefied natural gas shipments. The sharp decline reflects the growing security risks facing commercial vessels.

articles.title: Oil Prices Rise as Saudi Pipeline Remains Offline
articles.content: Oil prices moved higher on Tuesday as traders assessed the effect of continuing attacks and the disruption of Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline. Brent crude rose to around $106.93 a barrel, while US West Texas Intermediate reached about $102.65. The Saudi pipeline can normally transport around 4 million barrels per day to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, providing an alternative route around Hormuz.

articles.title: Houthi Attacks Add to Saudi Energy Security Concerns
articles.content: Iran-aligned Houthi forces have launched another wave of attacks against Saudi Arabia while strengthening positions along Yemen's Red Sea coast. Gulf Arab states have also postponed planned talks with Iran. The combination of military escalation and stalled diplomacy is increasing concern about the security of regional energy infrastructure and international shipping.

articles.title: Dangote Refinery IPO Continues to Attract Investor Attention
articles.content: Dangote Petroleum Refinery's initial public offering is underway in Nigeria. The company is offering 4.1 billion shares at ₦525 per share, targeting about ₦2.15 trillion, or approximately $1.6 billion. Reuters describes the transaction as Africa's largest IPO. The refinery currently operates at 700,000 barrels per day and plans to expand capacity to 1.4 million barrels per day over the next three years.

articles.title: Nigeria SEC Warns Investors Over Dangote IPO Fraud
articles.content: Nigeria's Securities and Exchange Commission has urged investors to exercise caution as interest in the Dangote Refinery IPO grows. The SEC says investors should obtain information from official channels and make payments only through designated and approved subscription platforms. The regulator also warns against unsolicited WhatsApp messages, social-media advertisements, fake websites and anyone promising guaranteed allocations.

articles.title: Sweden Election Leaves Centre-Left Ahead but Coalition Talks Loom
articles.content: Sweden's centre-left opposition remains in front following Sunday's parliamentary election. Preliminary results reported by Reuters showed the centre-left bloc ahead of Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson's right-wing bloc by three seats, 176 to 173. The far-right Sweden Democrats also suffered a significant setback. However, the final result and negotiations between potential coalition partners will determine who can form the next government.

articles.title: Ukraine Open to Conditional Energy Ceasefire
articles.content: Ukraine has expressed conditional support for a US-proposed halt to attacks on Russian and Ukrainian energy infrastructure. President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said Kyiv could support the arrangement if Washington can establish that Russia is genuinely committed to a reliable and lasting ceasefire. Ukraine has not treated the proposal as a completed agreement.

articles.title: Ukraine War Continues to Pressure European Security
articles.content: The Russia-Ukraine war remains a major security issue for Europe. The conflict continues to affect energy markets, military planning and transport infrastructure. Ukraine's attacks on Russian energy facilities have also become part of the wider dispute over fuel supplies, while Moscow continues to strike Ukrainian infrastructure.

articles.title: AI Stocks Remain Under Pressure
articles.content: Technology markets remain unsettled following renewed warnings about the risks associated with rapid artificial intelligence development. Reuters reported that AI-related stocks fell sharply across several markets after leading industry figures called for greater caution. Investors are also questioning whether enormous spending on chips, data centres and AI infrastructure will deliver sufficient long-term returns.

articles.title: Energy Shock Could Feed Into Household Costs
articles.content: The economic consequences of the Middle East crisis could extend beyond petrol prices. If shipping and energy disruptions continue, businesses may face higher transport, insurance and production costs. These pressures can eventually reach consumers through fuel, food, manufactured goods, aviation and household expenses, while central banks face a more difficult inflation environment.

articles.title: Nigeria's Domestic Refining Capacity Gains Strategic Importance
articles.content: The disruption to international oil routes highlights the importance of domestic refining capacity for African economies that depend on imported petroleum products. Nigeria's Dangote refinery is particularly significant because its planned expansion could increase domestic refining capacity and potentially strengthen the country's position in regional fuel markets.

articles.title: Global Markets Watch Oil and Geopolitical Risks
articles.content: International investors are monitoring the Middle East closely as higher oil prices combine with uncertainty over shipping routes, interest rates and global economic growth. Asian technology shares have also faced pressure following concerns about the pace and cost of artificial intelligence development.

morningSummary: Good morning. The global energy crisis is intensifying as shipping through the Strait of Hormuz falls to critically low levels. Only four commodity vessels crossed the waterway on Monday, compared with around 125 daily transits before the conflict. Brent crude has risen to around $106.93 a barrel while US WTI is around $102.65. Saudi Arabia's East-West oil pipeline also remains offline following attacks. In Nigeria, the Dangote Refinery IPO is attracting major public attention, while the Securities and Exchange Commission warns investors to use only authorised subscription channels. Sweden's centre-left bloc remains ahead after Sunday's close election, while Ukraine says it could support a conditional energy ceasefire with Russia if Moscow demonstrates genuine commitment. Meanwhile, renewed Houthi attacks and postponed Gulf-Iran talks are adding to concerns about the wider regional conflict.
bigQuestion: If the Strait of Hormuz remains severely disrupted for weeks, how much more could households eventually pay for fuel, food, transport and everyday essentials?
